group: Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk
question:
Patient note:
A 69-year-old man presented to the musculoskeletal peri-operative clinic four days before a scheduled arthroscopic repair of a chronic full-thickness supraspinatus tear that has limited overhead reach and interrupted sleep despite dedicated physical therapy, activity modification, and three ultrasound-guided subacromial corticosteroid injections; the orthopedic sports service anticipates a beach-chair position, three small portal sites, approximately 90 minutes of anesthesia time, minimal blood loss, and a single night of observation on the orthopedic ward with sling immobilization and formal physiotherapy beginning the following morning. He drove himself from a neighboring town, opted for the stairs rather than the elevator from the parking deck, and spoke in complete sentences at the registration desk, noting that shoulder pain—not breathlessness—forces him to rest after mowing half of his quarter-acre lawn, although he remains able to climb one flight of stairs to his bedroom while carrying a laundry basket without pausing. Twelve years ago he experienced sudden substernal pressure radiating to the left arm while shoveling heavy snow; peak troponin I rose to 7.6 ng/mL, emergent coronary angiography identified a 95 % proximal right-coronary-artery lesion that was treated with a drug-eluting stent, and dual antiplatelet therapy was continued for one year. He has had no recurrent chest discomfort, and a treadmill stress echocardiogram performed nine months ago reached 8 metabolic equivalents without ischemia or arrhythmia while he remained on his usual dose of metoprolol succinate 50 mg each morning. He has never been hospitalized for lower-extremity edema, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, or weight gain suggesting ventricular failure, and serial transthoracic echocardiograms ordered by his cardiologist during annual visits have demonstrated a stable left-ventricular ejection fraction of 55 % with normal diastolic parameters. Type 2 diabetes mellitus, diagnosed at age 55 when fasting plasma glucose exceeded 140 mg/dL, is currently managed with insulin glargine 28 units at 2200 h and insulin lispro dosed at a 1-unit-per-12-gram carbohydrate ratio before meals; finger-stick logs displayed on his smartphone show pre-breakfast readings between 100 and 160 mg/dL during the past month with no documented hypoglycemia, and the most recent hemoglobin A1c three months earlier was 7.4 %. Hypertension first identified two decades ago is controlled with lisinopril 10 mg nightly in addition to the beta-blocker, yielding home pressures that average 124/72 mm Hg. Hyperlipidemia is treated with rosuvastatin 20 mg nightly; his last lipid panel revealed an LDL of 78 mg/dL. He denies transient monocular blindness, speech disturbance, focal weakness, carotid intervention, seizure, or syncope. Pulmonary history is limited to mild seasonal allergic rhinitis managed with intranasal fluticasone; he quit cigarette smoking 25 years ago after a 15-pack-year exposure and now drinks a 12-ounce light beer with weekend dinners, denying recreational drug use. Previous operations include an uncomplicated laparoscopic cholecystectomy at age 50 and a right inguinal hernia repair at 63 without anesthetic difficulties. Family history is notable for a father who required coronary bypass at 68 and a mother who lived to 86 with diet-controlled diabetes; no close relatives suffered early stroke. Review of systems today is negative for fever, night sweats, paroxysmal cough, wheeze, palpitations, exertional dizziness, claudication, abdominal pain, melena, dysuria, or unintentional weight change. After five minutes of seated rest, vital signs in the right arm read 126/70 mm Hg, regular pulse 68 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98 % on room air, and oral temperature 36.7 °C; he measures 175 cm in height, weighs 84 kg, and has a body-mass index of 27.4 kg/m². He appears well nourished and in no acute distress. Jugular venous pulsation is not visible at 45°, carotid upstrokes are brisk without bruit, and the point of maximal impulse is palpable in the fifth intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line without displacement. First and second heart sounds are crisp with no gallop or murmur. Lungs are clear to percussion and auscultation throughout. The abdomen is soft and nontender with well-healed laparoscopic scars and no hepatosplenomegaly. Extremities are warm with 2+ dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses bilaterally and no edema. Examination of the right shoulder shows atrophy of the infraspinatus fossa, painful arc from 90° to 120°, positive Jobe test, and intact distal neurovascular status; gait is steady. Airway assessment documents Mallampati class II view, inter-incisor gap 4 cm, thyromental distance 7 cm, and full cervical range of motion. Pre-operative laboratory studies drawn one hour prior reveal hemoglobin 13.5 g/dL, hematocrit 40 %, platelet count 238 × 10⁹/L, white blood cell count 6.4 × 10⁹/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 26 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 1.71 mg/dL, corresponding to an estimated glomerular filtration rate of approximately 47 mL/min/1.73 m²; fasting plasma glucose drawn in the same sample measures 118 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase 26 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 23 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 92 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.1. A twelve-lead electrocardiogram obtained today shows normal sinus rhythm at 66 beats per minute, Q waves in leads II, III, and aVF consistent with the prior infarction, and no acute ST-segment deviation compared with a tracing from last year. Upright postero-anterior chest radiography demonstrates a normal cardiomediastinal silhouette and clear lung fields without pleural effusion. The anesthesia plan reviewed with the patient includes balanced general anesthesia supplemented by an ultrasound-guided interscalene block, continuation of metoprolol and lisinopril on the morning of surgery, reduction of the glargine dose by 20 % the preceding evening, withholding rapid-acting insulin and solid food after midnight with hourly intra-operative point-of-care glucose checks, and application of sequential compression stockings with postoperative low-dose subcutaneous heparin to mitigate venous thromboembolism risk. After teach-back, he accurately repeated fasting instructions, insulin adjustments, and early mobilization goals and voiced willingness to proceed with repair to regain pain-free overhead function.

Question: What is the patient's score of the Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Revised Cardiac Risk Index assigns 1 point for each of six preoperative criteria:
- High-risk surgery (intraperitoneal, intrathoracic, or suprainguinal vascular): shoulder arthroscopy is none of these → 0.
- Ischemic heart disease: prior myocardial infarction with coronary stenting → 1, despite the subsequent negative stress test.
- History of congestive heart failure: none documented → 0.
- Cerebrovascular disease: no prior stroke or TIA documented → 0.
- Preoperative insulin treatment: uses insulin glargine and lispro → 1.
- Serum creatinine >2.0 mg/dL: creatinine is 1.71 mg/dL → 0.
Sum: 0 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 1 + 0 = 2.
Final answer: 2
